# NZ First Announces Immigration Reform Policies

*Friday, 11 September 2026, 7:15 am Press Release: New Zealand First Party* — [https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA2609/S00118/nz-first-announces-immigration-reform-policies.htm](https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA2609/S00118/nz-first-announces-immigration-reform-policies.htm)

## Full text

New Zealand First has today announced a number of campaign policies that will make sweeping changes to current immigration laws.

New Zealand's immigration system must serve New Zealand and New Zealanders.

For too long, governments have relied on immigration to drive headline economic growth and cheap labour. The result has been greater pressure on housing, infrastructure and public services, increased competition for entry-level jobs, and declining public confidence that immigration is being managed in the national interest.

Population growth must not outpace our ability to build the country.

New Zealand First will substantially reduce non-essential immigration and restore the principle that immigration is a privilege, not a right.

New Zealand is more than an economy. It is a nation with its own history, institutions and way of life.

Immigration policy should strengthen social cohesion and encourage integration into a shared national community.

The foundation of any proper immigration system in our country should be the value placed on New Zealand citizenship.

New Zealand needs to start viewing our citizenship as most other countries around the world do - it is a privilege that comes with special and unique rights and identity.

We need to understand the importance of a country’s citizenship and the reasons why we must protect and enhance what it means to be a New Zealander.

This does not take away from the ability for migrants looking to move here, contribute, and help build our country from showing total commitment and patriotism for New Zealand by becoming a citizen.

Even the most basic of privileges and rights in any country like voting has become more like an expectation for all, rather than a unique right for New Zealanders.

In addition to the already announced policies of citizen’s only voting and citizen’s only NZ Super, New Zealand First will introduce the following policies in the next term of government:

· Birthright Citizenship – New Zealand First will update birthright citizenship requirements, so that only the children of citizens will be automatically entitled to New Zealand citizenship at birth.

· Asylum Seeker Changes - New Zealand First will reform the asylum seeker system, updating current settings so that they are fair, consistent, and fit for purpose. Protected person status will become temporary by design, subject to ongoing assessment.

o Any person who seeks asylum while in New Zealand on a working-class visa will be ineligible to do so.

o Asylum claimants will not be able to use the temporary work rights granted during the assessment period as a stepping stone to another visa.

· Permanent Resident and Citizenship Qualifying Period Adjustments - New Zealand First will double the required period to qualify for citizenship from five years to a minimum of ten years. The qualifying period for permanent residence will be extended from two to five years.

· Citizenship and Permanent Residence Application Fees – New Zealand First will increase the cost of applying for New Zealand citizenship and permanent residence to reflect its value and to better fund the wider immigration system.

· Welfare Stand-Down Period - New Zealand First will implement a 10-year welfare stand-down period for all visa holders, meaning non-citizens will be ineligible for jobseeker, accommodation supplement, or any other benefits during their first 10 years in New Zealand.

· Broadened Ability to Deport - New Zealand First will widen the criteria for deportation liability to cover any offence for which imprisonment is available as a sentence - with automatic deportation for those found guilty of violent or sexual crimes, found guilty of fraud, participating in an organised criminal group, money laundering, aiding and abetting under the Immigration Act, or migrant exploitation.

· Resident Visa Cap Referendum - New Zealand First will hold a referendum on the introduction of a legislated annual cap on the number of resident visas issued each year. Included in the Resident Visa Cap Referendum will be:

o A resident visa cap of 20,000 per year.

o Linking immigration settings directly to infrastructure capacity.

o Requiring major population growth to occur only where infrastructure already exists or is fully funded and scheduled for delivery.

o Stopping councils being forced to adapt to central government planning where local infrastructure cannot support it.

o Development of a 30-year Population Plan to coordinate immigration, housing and infrastructure planning.

· Social Housing for Citizens First – New Zealand First will ensure that social housing will be made available to citizens first and foremost.

· Chronic Overstayers – New Zealand First will implement a 24-month amnesty for overstayers to self-deport with no restrictions on applications to return.

o Any overstayer found past the clemency period has lapsed will be deported and permanently ineligible to apply for any visa in the future.

o In recognition of our commitment to our enduring Pacific relations, we will allow for a 24-month clemency period to facilitate any Pacific overstayer to apply to remain in the country legally on a valid visa. This will apply only to overstayers of Pacific origin.

· Student Visa Holders – New Zealand First will ensure student visa holders intending to transition to another visa will be required to leave before reapplying for another visa from abroad.

· Removal of Automatic Work Rights for Student Visa Holders – New Zealand First will remove the automatic work rights for international students and stop our kiwi jobs being taken by foreign students.

o Export education was designed to allow foreign students to come here, their economy pay for their education, and go back. It was not designed to allow them to take jobs off kiwis, have our economy pay for their education, and then to use the visa to move on to residence or work.

o It will be mandatory for any international student who wants to work in New Zealand while they study to apply under strict conditions to work. First and foremost, those job opportunities cannot be taken from New Zealanders looking for work.

· Immigration Ministerial Portfolio - It is imperative that a New Zealand First Minister holds the Immigration portfolio when part of the next coalition government to ensure the oversight, control and reform of the immigration system.

New Zealanders have the right to determine the future size and character of their country.

This set of polices is about taking back control of the future of our country and valuing our unique citizenship the way it should be - just like the vast majority of other countries do around the world.

Notes:

### 1: Citizens Only Voting (ANNOUNCED 5/07/2026)

### Only New Zealand Citizens should vote in our elections.

Current law allows permanent residents to vote in New Zealand’s elections[1].This makes New Zealand one of the few countries that extends this right to non-citizens.

Voting is the most fundamental expression of democratic participation. Extending that right to non-citizens dilutes what it means to be a New Zealander and removes a meaningful incentive to apply for citizenship.

New Zealand is an outlier among comparable nations. The vast majority of countries prohibit non-citizens from voting in national elections. That's the global default (Australia included).

Very few countries extend equal voting rights to non-citizens in national elections. Under current settings, permanent residents become eligible to vote after just one year of residence, lower than any comparable democratic peer.

This setting change would simply align our rules with the overwhelming international norm.

### 2: Superannuation for Citizens only (ANNOUNCED 6/9/2026)

### We will ensure that only citizens will be eligible to receive Superannuation.

New Zealand Superannuation is a commitment to Kiwis that have spent their lives working and contributing to this country. Our population is ageing and the cost of the scheme is increasing. However, we believe it should remain universal for all New Zealander citizens.

However, current settings allow for non-citizens to receive Superannuation:

“You may qualify for NZ Super if you: are 65 or older, and either: are a New Zealand (NZ) citizen, are a NZ permanent resident, or hold an NZ residence class visa, are ordinarily resident in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau when you apply, and have lived in New Zealand for a certain amount of time.”[2]

A non-citizen who arrives later in life and obtains permanent residence has the same entitlements as a citizen who has spent decades paying their share of taxes. We don’t think this is a fair or reasonable arrangement.

The cost of this decision is growing. In 2025, the government spend on superannuation for new migrants hit a billion dollars a year - roughly $20 million NZD per week[3].

Tightening eligibility to citizens only will reduce long-term pressure on the scheme, protect it for future generations for citizens, and provide a further incentive for permanent residents to pursue citizenship. Those who wish to retire here and access superannuation within the rules are welcome to do so - as citizens.

All non-citizens that currently receive New Zealand superannuation will not be impacted by this change – a 24-month grace period will apply, so that those seeking citizenship have ample time to do so prior to this change taking effect.

This adjustment will not infringe upon the rights of citizens of countries with which we have social security agreements already in place (also known as SSAs).

### 3: Birthright Citizenship

We will update birthright citizenship requirements, so that only the children of citizens will be automatically entitled to New Zealand citizenship at birth.

Under our current rules, newborns qualify as a citizen if, at the time of birth, at least one parent met one of these conditions (from govt.nz)[4]:

You are only a citizen if, when you were born, at least 1 of your parents was:

a New Zealand citizen, or

had a visa that allowed them to reside in New Zealand indefinitely.

For context, the Citizenship Amendment Act 2005 had previously removed unrestricted birthright citizenship, by requiring that the at least one parent be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident[5].

We believe that only the children of citizens should automatically receive citizenship at birth.

This further change is necessary because of the relative ease by which current permanent residence is attained. After just two years, migrants in some roles are able to apply for permanent residence. Children born after this point currently qualify for New Zealand citizenship automatically, even when their parents are not citizens.

The impact of this has been profound. The proportion of children born to permanent residents has rapidly grown within recent years. In combination with our previous policies, this would provide another incentive to apply for full citizenship. This would align our settings with other countries like Austria, Denmark, Japan and China, among (many) others.

### 4: Asylum Seeker Changes

New Zealand First will reform the asylum seeker system, updating current settings so that they are fair, consistent, and fit for purpose. Protected person status will become temporary by design, subject to ongoing assessment.

Over the past several decades, globalisation and mass migration have reshaped the immigration landscape in ways that our current approach was never designed to accommodate.

Asylum claims have continued to rise in recent times, reaching a record 2,345 in 2023. Meanwhile, the system's ability to process them has deteriorated. In 2019, 68% of claims reached a decision within the year. By 2023, that figure had fallen to 30%. Claims remained elevated at 2,270 in 2024/25. Of those who withdraw their claims, a third do so at the same time as lodging an application for a different New Zealand visa[6]. Current settings provide insufficient tools to distinguish genuine protection needs from those using the process as an alternative immigration pathway.

Currently, anyone can make an asylum claim. Each undergoes assessment, and where it succeeds, the claimant is granted refugee or protected person status. Refugees and protected persons can apply for permanent residence following recognition by a Refugee and Protection Officer or the New Zealand citizenship after 5 years of residence. They are meanwhile eligible to access employment, income support, and public health services, the same as New Zealand residents or citizens[7].

New Zealand First believes protected persons and refugees should instead be granted a renewable 24-month residence permit, temporary by design, with extensions considered individually according to each claimant's ongoing circumstances.

Where the genuine need for safe harbour has lapsed, because conditions in the country of origin have improved, that refugee status will end, and the individual will be returned home when conditions allow.

This model draws on the approach adopted by Denmark. Refugee status in Denmark is temporary and subject to review every 30 months, with settlement only available after an extended qualifying period.[8] Denmark reduced its asylum claims by more than 90% over a decade using this framework.

Any person who seeks asylum while in New Zealand on a working-class visa will be ineligible to do so. We do not consider these claims legitimate and will not accept them for asylum consideration.

New Zealand First will also legislate to prevent asylum claimants from using the temporary work rights granted during the assessment period as a stepping stone to other visa classes. Under current settings, individuals who lodge a claim are granted temporary work rights for the duration of the assessment process, a period that sometimes can last up to two and a half years[9]. This is exploitative and not in the spirit of the asylum seeker system.

Asylum claims are often used as a mechanism in exploitation; the visa holder is provided a statement to sign to lodge a claim and then become obligated to the facilitator of the claim process. It effectively creates a servitude relationship because the claimant is party to a fraudulent claim. As noted, it gives them up to 2.5 years of working rights while the claim is processed.

### 5: Permanent Resident and Citizenship Qualifying Period Adjustments

New Zealand First will double the required period to qualify for citizenship from five years to a minimum of ten years.

The qualifying periods for permanent residence will be extended from two to five years. We will also extend the qualifying period for New Zealand Citizenship from five to ten years.

Current rules allow for applications for Permanent Residence after holding a Resident Visa for just two years (with a minimum of 184 days in-country per year)[10]. The current pathway to full citizenship requires five years on any resident class visa.

In practice, the entire journey from arriving in New Zealand to holding a New Zealand passport can take just five years. Our current pathways are comparatively short when compared to similar nations.

How we compare:

United Kingdom: The standard path to Indefinite Leave to Remain (UK's equivalent of permanent residence) takes five years, followed by a further year before citizenship eligibility - six years total[11]

Japan: Recently updated the standard citizenship qualifying period to 10 years (previously 5)[12]. This brings it into line with the pathway to permanent residence, which is also 10 years.

Denmark: Permanent residence is available after eight years of continuous lawful residence on a temporary permit, with a four-year accelerated pathway available pending additional requirements[13]. Normally, for acquiring citizenship, it is a condition that you have been a resident continuously for 9 years[14].

Austria: Citizenship requires ten years of legal and uninterrupted residence, including five years as a resident[15]

Australia: Citizenship requires four years of residence (including one year as a permanent resident)[16]

Canada: Citizenship requires three years of physical presence within a five-year window, after obtaining permanent residence[17]

Italy, Spain: Require five years of continuous residence for permanent residence[18]. Also require ten years for naturalisation[19][20]

Portugal: Recently raised its residency requirements for citizenship from 5 to 10 years for non EU citizens[21].

Switzerland: Residents become eligible for permanent residence after 10 years of lawful residence in Switzerland[22].

Extending the qualifying period for permanent residence from two to five years, and period thereafter for citizenship from five to ten years ensures that newcomers are awarded on the basis of sustained, demonstrated commitment to our country.

### 6: Citizenship and Permanent Residence Application Fees

The cost of applying for New Zealand citizenship and permanent residence will be increased to reflect its value and to better fund the wider immigration system.

New Zealand citizenship by grant currently costs NZD $641 for adults[23]. This remains low by international standards, and recent increases were primarily driven by the need to cover processing costs.

Citizenship is the permanent commitment to New Zealand, entitling the holder the right to vote, to hold a New Zealand passport with all its privileges, and to pass that citizenship onto children. Under our policy, meeting specific time demands, would also entitle you to superannuation. The cost structure should reflect that.

Revenue generated through higher application fees can be directed toward processing backlogs, enforcement, and other crucial parts of the immigration system, reducing the burden on general taxpayers. This will include properly resourcing the asylum claims system, ensuring that claims and appeals are dealt with more quickly.

For these reasons, we propose increasing the cost of citizenship by grant to $950 to adequately reflect the value offered by being a New Zealand citizen. We propose a similar increase to Permanent Residence Class Visas (currently at $315[27], will be raised to $630).

A twenty-four-month grace period will apply prior to the new citizen application fee structure taking effect, providing ample opportunity for those already here and planning on applying for citizenship by grant to do so.

### 7: 10-year Welfare Stand Down Period for Visa Holders:

New Zealand First will implement a 10-year welfare stand-down period for all visa holders, meaning non-citizens will be ineligible for jobseeker, accommodation supplement, or any other benefits during their first 10 years in New Zealand. We believe that new residents should actually contribute to our country before being eligible for taxpayer support.

This is about attracting migrants who we need, not who need us.

New Zealand taxpayers should be protected from government decisions that have effectively imported poverty through settings that result in dependents and spouses being reliant on the main visa holder where salary settings are not sufficient to support dependents.

New Zealand would not be alone in applying this principle. Australia imposes a four-year waiting period on most newly arrived permanent residents before they can access certain welfare payments[28]. The United Kingdom also applies a habitual residence test before migrants can access income-related benefits.

### 8: Broadened Ability to Deport

We will widen the criteria for deportation liability to cover any offence for which imprisonment is available as a sentence - with automatic deportation for those found guilty of violent or sexual crimes, or found guilty of fraud, participating in an organised criminal group, money laundering, aiding and abetting under the Immigration Act or migrant exploitation.

Under current settings, deportation is only activated at specific sentencing thresholds. Section 161 of the Immigration Act 2009 establishes a tiered framework for determining when holders of resident and permanent resident visas who have committed criminal offences become liable for deportation. Each tier weighs two factors: how long the person has held their residence class visa, and how serious the offence is[29] [30].

This means a non-citizen can be convicted of a criminal offence and potentially face no immigration consequences whatsoever, simply because their sentence falls below an arbitrary line. This is not an outcome that serves New Zealanders economically or socially.

If a court has determined that an offence is serious enough to warrant the possibility of imprisonment (including rape and sexual offending, serious violent crime, migrant exploitation, domestic violence, and offences involving weapons or organised criminal association) that should be sufficient to instantly trigger deportation liability for any non-citizen post-prison term, regardless of the period that they have held a visa.

We will also amend the law so that any non-citizen specifically found guilty of committing a sexual or violent crime or found guilty of fraud or migrant exploitation will have no avenue to appeal their deportation to the Immigration and Protection Tribunal on humanitarian grounds. This is currently an avenue available to migrants to appeal deportation decisions[31].

(N.B: This differentiates NZF policy from the ongoing Immigration (Enhanced Risk Management) Amendment Bill, which has passed its first reading and is at select committee[32]. The Amendment Bill extends the period of residence during which a person can be subject to liability for deportation from ten to twenty years[33]. We will remove any cap on deportation liability for serious crimes, and also extend the inability to appeal to Immigration and Protection Tribunal on humanitarian grounds to permanent residence holders, rather than just temporary visas[34]

### 9: Resident Visa Cap Referendum

New Zealand First will hold a referendum on the introduction of a legislated annual cap on the number of resident visas issued each year.

This policy is about one thing: the gap between how fast New Zealand is growing and how fast it is able to build and maintain the infrastructure, housing, public services, and jobs that growth demands. That gap is not sustainable, and it is not acceptable to continue widening it in the absence of any deliberate plan to manage that growth sustainably.

One of the largest recent drivers was a deliberate policy decision, not an organic trend. The previous Labour Government's 2021 Resident Visa scheme resulted in 212,649 new residence permits being granted.[35] At its peak, more than 10,000 residence visas per month were being approved[36]. Our public services were not designed to absorb that pace of growth. There should be checks in place to prevent something like this from occurring again under future governments.

The consequences are visible to every New Zealander: hospitals overwhelmed, housing unaffordable, doctors waiting lists growing, and infrastructure investment perpetually chasing a population that keeps outpacing it. Compounding this, Immigration New Zealand recorded 72,700 New Zealand citizen departures in the year ending September 2025, (and, more recently, 63,900 in the year ended June 2026). New Zealand is simultaneously importing people at an unprecedented rate and losing our own citizens at a record pace. That is not a sustainable or coherent population policy.

Australia has operated a similar model for decades - an annual cap, currently 185,000 places, split 70/30 between skilled migrants and family and humanitarian entrants[37]. Australia adjusts this figure annually against labour market conditions, housing capacity, and settlement infrastructure. It is a deliberate, managed system. We should do the same.

The United States maintains a cap on permanent residence, presently set at 675,000 visas per year, with employment and family categories set by Congress. Canada publishes an annual Immigration Levels Plan, calibrated against housing supply, healthcare capacity, and labour market need - and has recently reduced its targets in direct response to housing pressure.

What these countries share is a recognition that population growth driven by migration is a policy lever that must be carefully managed.

A resident visa cap of 20,000 per year represents a sustainable and manageable level, allowing New Zealand to continue attracting skilled migrants, meet its humanitarian obligations, while also giving public services and labour market the breathing room needed to recover.

The management of New Zealand's population should be a subject of deliberate public choice. The social consequences of unmanaged mass migration are visible in other developed nations. We have the opportunity and an obligation to future generations to do better.

Included in the Resident Visa Cap Referendum will be:

Linking immigration settings directly to infrastructure capacity.

Requiring major population growth to occur only where infrastructure already exists or is fully funded and scheduled for delivery.

Stopping councils being forced to adapt to central government planning where local infrastructure cannot support it.

Development of a 30-year Population Plan to coordinate immigration, housing and infrastructure planning.

Population growth must not outpace our ability to build the country.

For decades, governments have encouraged mass immigration without ensuring that the roads, water infrastructure, schools, hospitals and housing needed to support population growth were in place.

### 10: Social Housing for Citizens First

We believe that social housing should be made available to citizens first and foremost.

Demand for Social housing is under extreme pressure. As of June 2026, there were 19,002 applicants on the Housing Register[38]. Under current settings, social housing eligibility extends equally to citizens and permanent residents[39]. New Zealand First believes this requires adjustment. Citizenship represents the fullest expression of commitment to this country, and those who have made that commitment should be prioritised when it comes to state resources that are in short supply.

Those who have made the fullest commitment to this country and have gone through the naturalisation process and taken on the rights and responsibilities of citizenship, should be prioritised when state resources are being allocated.

For this reason, we will direct MSD to implement a prioritisation framework that places citizens at the front of the queue ahead of permanent residents when allocating social housing placements.

### 11: Chronic Overstayers

Immigration New Zealand estimates that 20,980 people are currently in New Zealand having unlawfully overstayed their visas[40]. This places additional pressure on public services and undermines the integrity of an immigration system that the vast majority navigate lawfully and in good faith.

A large portion of illegal overstayers originate from neighbouring Pacific island nations. It goes without saying that we share a unique and close bond with these countries. In recognition of our commitment to our enduring Pacific relations, we will allow for a 24-month clemency period to facilitate any Pacific overstayer to apply to remain in the country legally on a valid visa. This will apply only to overstayers of Pacific origin.

Any overstayer found past the clemency period has lapsed will be deported. These deported overstayers will be permanently ineligible to apply for any visa in the future, due to their heightened risk of reoffending.

We will also invest a further $50 million into frontline immigration compliance resourcing. This will ensure that Immigration NZ has the tools and the staff needed to cut into the growing number of chronic overstayers.

New Zealand First recognises that overstayers live in a vulnerable state with a higher likelihood of being victims of exploitation, trafficking, and forced labour. Investment in investigative resource and enforcement will provide opportunity for intervention and protections.

### 12: Student Visa Holders Must Reapply for Other Visas from Offshore

Student visa holders intending to transition to another visa will be required to leave before reapplying for another visa from abroad.

From the over 90,000 student visa holders enrolled in 2025, approximately 32,000 will move to a resident or work visa.

The student visa exists for a specific purpose: to allow foreigners to study. It does not (and should not) function as a backdoor to long-term residence. Requiring applicants to reapply from offshore closes this potential loophole whereby student visas are used as a staging ground for extended stays that was never the original intent of the education visa grant. For those who are genuinely committed to a long-term future here, departing to reapply presents no real issue.

The requirement applies only to those seeking to change their visa status, not to students completing their studies and departing as intended. This change protects the integrity of the student visa category.

### 13. Removal of Automatic Work Rights for Student Visa Holders

Export education was designed to allow foreign students to come here, pay for their education, and go back. It was not designed to allow them to take jobs off kiwis, and then to use the visa to move on to residence or work.

New Zealand’s current Youth Unemployment rate is approximately 22% and Youth Under-utilisation rate is approximately 37%.

That means approximately 70,000 15–24-year-old New Zealanders who are unemployed and actively looking for work.

documents/2026-09-13-winston-peters-spee.title: Winston Peters' Speech - \"Cool Heads, Rational Judgement\
documents/2026-09-13-winston-peters-spee.text:
# Winston Peters' Speech - "Cool Heads, Rational Judgement"

*Sunday, 13 September 2026, 2:54 pm Speech: New Zealand First Party* — [https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA2609/S00134/winston-peters-speech-cool-heads-rational-judgement.htm](https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA2609/S00134/winston-peters-speech-cool-heads-rational-judgement.htm)

## Full text

Rt Hon Winston Peters Takapuna Public Meeting Speech The Spencer Suites, Takapuna 2pm, 13 September 2026

### An Uncertain World

We are living through a hugely complex and challenging period.

This places an enormous premium on experience, and through experience, good judgements that protect New Zealand’s vital interests.

We take the world as it is, not as some cloistered varsity lecturer or woke leftie wants it to be. The record shows that we have exercised sound judgement when it has mattered most.

With experience comes prudence, and with diplomacy comes opportunity, and that is why we are guardedly optimistic that New Zealand will emerge from the serious global disruptions in a strong position to exploit every opportunity that we create or that comes our way.

### The State of the Economy

We all know the economy isn’t where it should be. We all know that, without having to be told because kiwis are struggling sometimes working two, even three jobs, just to make ends meet.

New Zealand First has constantly said that it will take time to turn our economy around.

We have been open about that - and when other parties at the last election said that they could fix it within three years – we said that was a mistake. We knew the damage done to the economy by the previous Labour government couldn’t be undone in three years.

We know it can be fixed – but it will take time.

We are making some positive movements as an economy in such uncertain times. But we can, and must, do better.

But to do much better, we need many more New Zealand First MPs in parliament.

Many, many, more.

Inflation is on the rise again, not nearly as bad as under Labour, but it is on the rise.

Interest rates are on the rise again, not nearly as bad as under Labour, but on the rise.

Our slow economic recovery has been set back by events in the Middle East and worsened overnight with the capture of the Red Sea port, thereby blocking Saudi Arabian Oil.

That said, stability in the middle east is likely to be restored more quickly than New Zealand’s economic return to recovery.

And that’s because, our government inherited a disaster of massive overborrowing, and spending not on production, not on wealth creation, not on employment, and not on exports, but purely on consumption.

And we're paying a massive price for that now.

We just had the COVID Inquiry showing the previous Labour government borrowed sixty billion dollars to deal with COVID, and yet they spent thirty billion of it on something else.

That is half of the sixty billion wasn’t spent on COVID. And you’re sitting in this audience and the mainstream media have told you what the thirty billion was wasted on.

We have turned the economy around - there is growth, but not nearly as much as we need.

The current economic climate and the reality of our situation just shows the sad thing about New Zealand over the past fifty years.

We went from being in the top three in the world to a non-competing economy.

Back then we had strong growth of over five percent a year, every year, and MPs who understood nationalism, who understood the national interest.

And then in 1984 we had the neoliberal experiment of Labour’s Roger Douglas and then National’s Ruth Richardson and the rest has been a massive disaster.

We became the victim of a totally unfettered free market - straight out of the neoliberal economic Milton Freidman textbook.

The left and right, Labour then National, went on to sell our assets, privatise our country, open our borders to mass immigration, open our society to every wild-west simpleton ideology – an ideology that has been proven over the past forty years to be an abject failure and purveyor of misery and struggle.

Only one party leader and one party – New Zealand First - has never subscribed to that ideology.

New Zealand First began because we opposed that ideology.

We have always believed in economic nationalism – where we own our country’s assets, where we have targeted government intervention, where we give a hand up in times of need, where our country gives capitalism a human face.

### NZFirst Immigration Policy

How many times has New Zealand First been attacked for being xenophobic and racist, look around the world – it calls to mind the quote from The Mikado “the idiot who praises with enthusiastic tone, all centuries but this and every country but his own.”

We need smart immigration policies – where we shift the dial to a highly skilled critical workforce that our country needs, and provide real reasons for these kiwis to stay in New Zealand to rebuild our country together. A system that consistently provides the skills we need domestically, working alongside the education system which fills the skills we need in our industries.

We need a system that focusses on the needs of the employers, industry, and kiwi workers.

Smart, not more, immigration.

Ladies and gentlemen, it may come as a surprise to most, but over 30% of all current New Zealand residents were not even born in New Zealand. That’s approaching a third of all who live in New Zealand weren’t born here. Thirty years ago, in the 1990’s it was just 14%.

On that same upward trend, without smart immigration policies, in as little as just another 15 or 20 years that percentage will be approaching 50% of people living here not being born here. That’s your children and grandchildren’s generation.

It’s not just about the number of migrants coming into our country, it is about all of those young, trained, driven, smart, working-age kiwis that are leaving.

Under Labour’s 2023 final year, they let in 132,000 new migrants, net. There was a record number of people leaving New Zealand to go to Australia last year and apply to be citizens – the most concerning statistic is that half of those so-called New Zealand citizens who left, were not even born in New Zealand.

New Zealand is being used as a steppingstone into Australia. We take them in, train them, up-skill them, look after their families, and they then move to Australia or elsewhere. How is this an effective immigration policy?

Ladies and gentlemen, the fact is, in the past four years around 622,000 new migrants have come to this country, with a net number of 165,000. That increase in our population is almost the size of Hamilton over just four years. But the past is not the most concerning part. It is where we could be headed without a smart immigration policy and what that means for the future of our country.

Concerns are growing, as to some of the people who have come here who don’t salute our flag, don’t honour the values of our country, don’t respect the people living here, don’t respect the right to have our own religion and freedom of speech. These are values that we need to fight to protect. If you don’t want to sign up to those values, don’t come.

People around the world are fearful as to where their countries are going – just look at States in America, the UK, Ireland, Germany, and recently in Australia - and New Zealanders are no different. They are more acutely aware of the problem we’re dealing with here than the politicians are.

They have seen the international circumstances of careless immigration policies transforming cities, changing cultures, changing centuries of development and social life, and people feel at risk because of it.

We believe in a country called New Zealand, with one law, one people, one flag, and one set of values that our forebears fought and died for. And if we are the only party willing to stand in the way of globalist politicians and bureaucrats trying to take our country away, then so be it.

### Immigration Policy

Two days ago New Zealand First announced a number of campaign policies that will make sweeping changes to current immigration laws.

Taxpayer owned TVNZ refuses to report anything we have said on this critical policy. Not one story or article.

New Zealand's immigration system must serve New Zealand and New Zealanders.

For too long, governments have relied on immigration to drive headline economic growth and cheap labour.

The result has been greater pressure on housing, infrastructure and public services, increased competition for entry-level jobs, and declining public confidence that immigration is being managed in the national interest.

Population growth must not outpace our ability to build the country.

New Zealand First will substantially reduce non-essential immigration and restore the principle that immigration is a privilege, not a right.

New Zealand is more than an economy. It is a nation with its own history, institutions and way of life.

New Zealand needs to start viewing our citizenship as most other countries around the world do - as a privilege that comes with special and unique rights and identity.

This does not take away from the ability for migrants looking to move here, contribute, and help build our country from showing total commitment and patriotism for New Zealand by becoming a citizen.

In addition to the already announced policies of citizen’s only voting and citizen’s only NZ Super, New Zealand First will introduce the following policies in the next term of government:

· Birthright Citizenship – New Zealand First will update birthright citizenship requirements, so that only the children of citizens will be automatically entitled to New Zealand citizenship at birth.

· Asylum Seeker Changes - New Zealand First will reform the asylum seeker system, updating current settings so that they are fair, consistent, and fit for purpose. Protected person status will become temporary by design, subject to ongoing assessment.

o Any person who seeks asylum while in New Zealand on a working-class visa will be ineligible to do so.

o Asylum claimants will not be able to use the temporary work rights granted during the assessment period as a stepping stone to another visa.

· Permanent Resident and Citizenship Qualifying Period Adjustments - New Zealand First will double the required period to qualify for citizenship from five years to a minimum of ten years. The qualifying period for permanent residence will be extended from two to five years.

· Citizenship and Permanent Residence Application Fees – New Zealand First will increase the cost of applying for New Zealand citizenship and permanent residence to reflect its value and to better fund the wider immigration system.

· Welfare Stand-Down Period - New Zealand First will implement a 10-year welfare stand-down period for all visa holders, meaning non-citizens will be ineligible for jobseeker, accommodation supplement, or any other benefits during their first 10 years in New Zealand.

· Broadened Ability to Deport - New Zealand First will widen the criteria for deportation liability to cover any offence for which imprisonment is available as a sentence - with automatic deportation for those found guilty of violent or sexual crimes, found guilty of fraud, participating in an organised criminal group, money laundering, aiding and abetting under the Immigration Act, or migrant exploitation.

· Resident Visa Cap Referendum - New Zealand First will hold a referendum on the introduction of a legislated annual cap on the number of resident visas issued each year. Included in the Resident Visa Cap Referendum will be:

o A resident visa cap of 20,000 per year.

o Linking immigration settings directly to infrastructure capacity.

o Requiring major population growth to occur only where infrastructure already exists or is fully funded and scheduled for delivery.

o Stopping councils being forced to adapt to central government planning where local infrastructure cannot support it.

o Development of a 30-year Population Plan to coordinate immigration, housing and infrastructure planning.

· Social Housing for Citizens First – New Zealand First will ensure that social housing will be made available to citizens first and foremost.

· Chronic Overstayers – New Zealand First will implement a 24-month amnesty for overstayers to self-deport with no restrictions on applications to return.

o Any overstayer found past the clemency period has lapsed will be deported and permanently ineligible to apply for any visa in the future.

o In recognition of our commitment to our enduring Pacific relations, we will allow for a 24-month clemency period to facilitate any Pacific overstayer to apply to remain in the country legally on a valid visa. This will apply only to overstayers of Pacific origin.

· Student Visa Holders – New Zealand First will ensure student visa holders intending to transition to another visa will be required to leave before reapplying for another visa from abroad.

· Removal of Automatic Work Rights for Student Visa Holders – New Zealand First will remove the automatic work rights for international students and stop our kiwi jobs being taken by foreign students.

o Export education was designed to allow foreign students to come here, their economy pay for their education, and go back. It was not designed to allow them to take jobs off kiwis, have our economy pay for their education, and then to use the visa to move on to residence or work.

o It will be mandatory for any international student who wants to work in New Zealand while they study to apply under strict conditions to work. First and foremost, those job opportunities cannot be taken from New Zealanders looking for work.

· Immigration Ministerial Portfolio - It is imperative that a New Zealand First Minister holds the Immigration portfolio when part of the next coalition government to ensure the oversight, control and reform of the immigration system.

You have the right to determine the future size and character of your country.

This set of polices is about taking back control of our country and valuing our unique citizenship the way it should be.

New Zealand First since our formation has been warning about mass immigration being used as a crutch for the economy and failing workforce planning for our own people.

In 2017 when we became part of the government immigration was dramatically cut back. In 2021, when we were no longer part of the government, the governments feet came totally off the brakes, and Labour governing with the Greens began approving 213,000 migrant visas in just 18 months.

Following Covid in 2022, the immigration department loosely approved nearly every application for residency in New Zealand.

And when Labour was unleashing these hundreds of thousands of new immigrants on New Zealand, the National Party and the Act Party said absolutely nothing.

As it says in the good book – “By their deeds you will know them”.

We need immigration to New Zealand. It has been an essential part of our history. But this should be smart controlled immigration policy – bringing in immigrants who we need, not who need us.

It will always bring the inevitable naval gazing by the other parties who would rather fill gaps in our economy and workforce with migrants, than train and maintain kiwis, and protect the “kiwi dream”.

The ‘kiwi dream’ belongs to kiwis who have worked hard for our country, invested time, sweat, pride, and belongs to the generations who share in our country’s history. It is not for just anybody around the world who decides to come to our great country for five minutes and claim what we have built just for their convenience.

Ladies and gentlemen, for decades you have heard other politicians gloating perversely that “diversity is a strength”.

You’ve heard them all say it.

And its false.

Because unity is a strength, not diversity. Diversity is weakness and disunity.

The choice is in your hands, not retail globalist politicians.

### Labour’s Mass Immigration Policy

Around three hours after New Zealand First announced our immigration policies on Friday, Labour decided to release theirs.

Except Labour was what you would expect – a bunch of empty words that want to sound like they are talking about immigration, but do exactly what they have always done – tinkered around the edges with a sprinkling of crazy global citizenship policies thrown in.

And by the way, Labour’s Twyford - he of the 100,000 KiwiBuild Homes, except there weren’t even 1000, had the temerity on the news on Friday night to accuse New Zealand First policies as being “racist” – this from the guy who created Labour’s immigration policy in 2017 by searching for ‘Chinese sounding names’ in the Auckland home owners register. Remember that?

Twyford said "Immigration should be planned around what New Zealand needs, and it should be managed in a way that's fair to everyone here and everyone who comes," – he must think New Zealanders are stupid, this is coming from the party that in 2023, alone, let in an extra 132,000 net new migrants.

An astonishing number. There is no person on the planet who thinks this type of number can be managed by our infrastructure.

They did it to disguise their failing economy and artificially boost demand. They had no care whatsoever for the long-term effect it would have on our country.

Labour is the party of mass immigration.

What is most concerning with what they announced, is that they said they would “set up a citizenship pathway for children born in New Zealand, and reviewing parent visa, health, and English-language rules”.

In other words, they want someone who has been here for five minutes to be able to have a child who will automatically become a citizen – which will give the immigrant parents the right to stay.

This is pure lunacy. They are treating our citizenship like it means nothing. They are saying our citizenship is just a spreadsheet exercise and box that needs to be ticked.

We in New Zealand First believe our citizenship is a privilege, not a right, and not just part of some bureaucratic machinery.

### Waitangi Tribunal / Greens Grocers

There have been policy announcements from other parties over the past week.

### Greens Grocers

The Greens new policy of Nationalising Private Supermarkets is textbook communism by stealth.

The Greens have gone full Soviet-style. The waiting queues will be kilometres long - just look at how it turned out in places like Venezuela.

The Green Party has literally stated that their government would “pass new laws forcing Woolworths and Foodstuffs to sell 120 existing stores and two major distribution centres” into public ownership.

And on dependant calculations their buying those shops for a quarter of their market value.

This is forcing private companies to sell their businesses to the government - it is not only nuts, it is the definition of communism.

The Greens are economic illiterates - this from Chloe who wants to be the Minister of Finance.

Chris Hipkins is waking up in cold sweats even before the election.

### Waitangi Tribunal

The Waitangi Tribunal is currently operating as a grievance make-work scheme and way out of scope of its original purpose when it was established.

Does it need to be abolished? Yes.

The Act Party also announced that it would abolish the Waitangi Tribunal once all settlements are completed.

But unfortunately the Act Party’s announcement comes straight out of Jim Bolger’s speech circa 1990 - where he said it will be wound up by 2014 once all settlements were completed. Remember that? “Once completed” means “sometime never”.

Sadly, the Act Party policy is the same illusion that Bolger had and doesn’t deal with the Tribunal.

New Zealand First’s plan is to deal with the Waitangi Tribunal once and for all – and we will be announcing this policy shortly.

### Willie Jackson Co-Governance / Māori Apprenticeships

Labour’s Willie Jackson on Q&A was asked if Labour was going to bring back co-governance.

Willie said yes, but “apparently co-governance scares people, so we might give it a new name”.

Whatever new name he wants to give it, it will still be:

Separatist.

Racist.

Apartheid.

Co-governance is the destruction of our democracy. That’s why New Zealand First opposes it.

Because we believe in one people, one flag, one country, one law for all.

That is why we announced a policy to abolish the unelected Independent Māori Statutory Board.

Labour is on a patronising separatist race to the bottom along with the Greens, Te Pati Māori, and Opportunity Party.

Our vision and values as a country should be based on need not race - the sooner we get rid of separatist thinking and work together as one people the sooner we will have a better future together as one people.

### Māori Party Destructive Bottom Lines

The Labour Party's coalition partner, the Māori Party, released a tax policy - they called a "bottom line".

They want to introduce a wealth tax, a massive corporate tax, a stamp duty, a property speculation tax, and an offshore speculation tax.

This is both a jobs killer and a business killer.

But guess what, surprise surprise, these wealth taxes don’t apply to Māori.

This is a policy for the taxpayer funded Māori elite, by the taxpayer funded Māori elite, from the taxpayer funded Māori elite.

All they have done is treat Māori with disdain, turn up to parliament once a month, and do a haka now and again in the House.

And who wants to sit with them at Cabinet with their extremist views? The Labour Party.

### Opportunity Party’s Communist Consultants

Another party the Labour Party wants to work with is the new Opportunity Party.

The Opportunity Party wants homeowners to pay 1.75% of your home’s land value every year, that’s on top of your local rates.

Now you will have to pay an annual rent to the government.

And when the leader of the Opportunity Party was asked how an old couple could afford a $20k land tax bill every year, she said “they will have to downsize their house to afford it”.

This is blisteringly ignorant. But it gets worse.

It will be used for a Universal Basic Income of $19,400 every year, for everyone, for life, even if they are not working.

Opportunity Party calls this ‘fairness’.

New Zealand First calls it ‘communism’.

And who wants to sit with them in Cabinet? The Labour Party.

### Green Party Debt Machine

The Greens want an $88 billion debt increase, and have a new policy bribe to give $2.4 billion to Marae – without any oversight or audit of taxpayers’ money.

This is inverse racism of the worst sort. They think they can use a bribe to get your vote. This doesn’t reflect respect for you, but sheer contempt for who you are.

The Greens are obsessed with race, gender, pronouns, and protests, performative politics, virtue signalling, and woke cancel culture, and they have completely lost sight of what their party once stood for.

### Old Labour Is Gone

Ladies and gentlemen, this is the stark truth. The Labour Party that you once knew, perhaps even supported, is no more.

That party is gone. All of these polices and parties they are willing to support are proof of that.

Can you imagine Helen Clark or Michael Cullen, or Bob Tizard or Peter Frazer signing up to this?

### Some Announced Bold Policies

We have announced a policy to break up the power companies, splitting the supermarket duopoly, creating a truly competitive New Zealand owned bank.

We have announced a policy to return mining royalties back to the regions.

We announced our KiwiSaver policy with automatic $1000 sign-up at birth, we will establish a $100 billion Future Fund that will invest in a thirty-year infrastructure plan for our country.

And we have announced a policy to ensure only citizens are allowed to vote in our country.

We will pull out of the Paris Accord.

We are going to have a referendum on the Maori seats, invest $1billion to find and extract our own oil and gas in our deep sea basins, we announced the ‘Kiwi Kids Grant’ that will support New Zealand citizens raising their first three children, through the first three years of their lives.

And while all the other parties argue about spending and taxation, New Zealand First is different.

We are talking about doubling our economy by 2050. Which is the only way we are going to be able to pay for the things that New Zealanders need.

### Covid Inquiry into Vaccine Injuries

We have announced establishing a proper transparent inquiry into those who were injured by the Covid 19 vaccine – so we can find out exactly what happened, who was responsible, and publicly hold them to account.

Why did 311,000 12-17 year olds get a second vaccination when Labour’s Hipkins and Verrall were told not to give it to them?

### The Choice On The Right

This year we have been packing the halls around the country with ordinary hardworking kiwi battlers who see the only party talking common sense.

They all see what makes New Zealand First different from every other party.

We are the only socially conservative party.

We are the only nationalist party.

We are the only patriotic party – a word that is now so often criticised. We stand proud to be patriots of New Zealand.

What’s most important, is that we are the only party that can counter-balance the present spectrum of extremists in parliament.

And we have the vitally experienced team and the bold policies to back it up.

New Zealand First is not just running in another election this year, we are running to save our country economically and socially from extremists.

### Conclusion

Ladies and gentlemen, we are all here because we love our country, and we are proud of it.

True democracy is a rare flower in the history of humanity.

Down thousands of years living in democracy with freedom is a historical rarity.

We have inherited a free country that our forebears fought and died for, and it’s our job to preserve it.

But only if we are proud of what we have inherited can we come together and move forward to shape the vision of our country’s future.

We live in a country that, at its core, traditional New Zealand values once saw us amongst the world’s leaders – hard work, fair pay, valuing our citizenship, building a sense of community, and knowing who we are as kiwis.

We must remember, New Zealand is the beneficiary of Western values, democracy, and the rule of law. And the advancement and enhancement of those principles have only occurred in those societies that have united together as one people - and who celebrate their nationhood instead of perpetuating division.

There is a lot of uncertainty around the world and at home, but we must keep hope alive that, with hard work and perseverance, tomorrow will be better.

We must never stop believing in New Zealand.

That is our vision and that is our mission.

To protect, to save, and to restore New Zealand’s place at the top of the world.

By putting New Zealand and New Zealanders first.

We are asking you to join us - and Party Vote New Zealand First.

# Common Sense Must Prevail For Retirement Village Reform

*Friday, 18 September 2026, 3:08 pm Press Release: New Zealand First Party* — [https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA2609/S00193/common-sense-must-prevail-for-retirement-village-reform.htm](https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA2609/S00193/common-sense-must-prevail-for-retirement-village-reform.htm)

## Full text

Today's announcement that the Retirement Villages Amendment Bill will be introduced next term delivers on New Zealand First's commitment to progress the Retirement Village review.

"New Zealand First is focused on improving life for seniors and delivering common sense reform," says New Zealand First MP Casey Costello.

Around 50,000 of New Zealand's 950,000 seniors live in retirement villages, and most are happy with that choice. Retirement villages are an important housing option for older New Zealanders, often improving quality of life and health outcomes, while adding valuable aged care capacity.

"Seniors need more choice and more security. New Zealand First will deliver legislation that protects residents where needed, supports more housing options, and recognises the sector's role in aged care," says Ms Costello.

"This is not about one single fix. It is about making practical changes that improve outcomes for seniors."

Proposals for three-month buy-backs with retrospective application would destabilise the sector, raise costs for future residents, and undermine the security current residents value.

"Three-month buy-backs are political posturing. They would damage the sector and make residents more vulnerable," says Ms Costello.

Reform must protect residents, support investment, and keep the sector sustainable for the tens of thousands of seniors who rely on it.

"New Zealand First will ensure practical retirement village legislation is delivered -common sense reform that protects both the sector and the seniors who call it home."

documents/2026-09-20-nz-first-campaign-a.text:
# NZ First Campaign Announcement: The Plan To “Make NZ Healthy”

*Sunday, 20 September 2026, 2:44 pm Press Release: New Zealand First Party* — [https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA2609/S00205/nz-first-campaign-announcement-the-plan-to-make-nz-healthy.htm](https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA2609/S00205/nz-first-campaign-announcement-the-plan-to-make-nz-healthy.htm)

## Full text

New Zealand First is today announcing the first part of a plan for a directional change of the health system and to ‘Make NZ Healthy”.

No one will disagree that we have a crisis in our health system. Over the past three years we have been listening to kiwis, public health experts, doctors, and scientists.

We have an epidemic of chronic illness impacting the lives of one million kiwis, overwhelming our hospitals, and putting unsustainable pressure on our economy.

It’s time for new thinking with a bold shift from treating illness to preventing it.

Other parties’ solution is to announce more spending on medicines and treatment, rather than properly investigate, research, and fund preventions of the causes and alternate healthy lifestyle solutions.

New Zealand is currently spending $33 billion a year on health and nearly all of it is spent treating people after they are sick.

New Zealand’s own research shows that 59% of health spending is spent on treating chronic diseases like diabetes and heart disease, the very illnesses that can largely be prevented - only 1.75% is spent on preventing them in the first place.

That’s not a health system. That is an ambulance at the bottom of the cliff, and New Zealanders are paying for the ambulance.

Spending more in a Health Budget on the ever-increasing market for drugs will never be enough. We need to solve the underlying reasons for the increasing number of chronic illnesses our strained system is now treating.

New Zealand First will shift the focus of healthcare from treating illness to preventing it. By supporting healthier lifestyles, early intervention and stronger communities, we can keep New Zealanders healthier, reduce pressure on hospitals, and build a more sustainable health system.

Having adequate funding for medicines is an essential part of the health system but should not be the goal nor seen as the solution – it will only ever manage the decline of our country’s health.

A small proportion of what we currently spend treating established disease could fund serious independent research into whether inexpensive nutritional interventions can help prevent diseases developing or progressing in the first place.

If it reduces diabetes, cardiovascular disease, mental illness, infection or hospital admissions by even a modest amount, the return will dwarf the investment.

That is what prevention should mean.

We spend billions treating sickness - it is time we invested a small fraction of that money in finding out how much sickness we can prevent.

New Zealand First will:

1. Put prevention back at the heart of healthcare.

2. Have a strong focus on metabolic health, the key driver of chronic illness.

3. Ensure that informed consent is a core part of quality healthcare.

4. Recognise that consumer choice is what leads to healthier decisions.

5. Promote nutrition from primary school to medical school.

6. Require a full independent review of our dietary guidelines.

7. Reduce administrative burden and restore professional autonomy in General Practice.

8. Support our GPs by bringing health coaches into primary care.

9. Find better ways to acknowledge our nurses.

10. Fund our New Zealand scientists to assess nutritional interventions for preventing and treating mental illness.

11. Remove Medsafe/Pharmac barriers to recognised safe nutrients.

12. Invest in hospital trials to assess the effectiveness of intravenous vitamin C pre- and post-surgery for preventing and treating infections.

13. Fund a review of vitamin D and determine optimal levels for maintaining health.

14. Support farmers and growers by investing in agricultural innovation that improves productivity, soil health, sustainability and resilience while researching practical alternatives to potentially harmful agricultural sprays.

15. Back our organic producers, cut unnecessary barriers, encourage investment and innovation, and grow new markets so New Zealand’s organic industry can create more jobs, strengthen regional communities, and deliver greater value from our land.

We need a serious direction change of what our health system does and how it is funded.

This is just the first campaign announcement in the larger plan to ‘Make NZ Healthy”.

# NZFirst To Campaign On 20% Tax Rate For SMEs

*Thursday, 24 September 2026, 1:01 pm Press Release: New Zealand First Party* — [https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA2609/S00261/nzfirst-to-campaign-on-20-tax-rate-for-smes.htm](https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA2609/S00261/nzfirst-to-campaign-on-20-tax-rate-for-smes.htm)

## Full text

New Zealand First is announcing today it will campaign on lowering the company tax rate for SMEs to 20% for companies with turnover under $30million, from its current 28% tax rate.

This is a much-needed bold step to encourage more investment by our small businesses that will create higher productivity, expand their business, and employ more New Zealanders.

Corporate taxes can reduce productivity, particularly in entrepreneurial and innovative sectors. Lower company tax rates can improve long-run productivity growth, and stimulate the creation of new companies.

A lower tax rate leaves additional cash available for reinvestment and reduces reliance on bank debt.

It is estimated that the tax reduction will have an initial annual fiscal cost of approximately $1billion. This will be more than covered in the medium term by more companies collectively paying a lower tax rate, higher employment, a growing economy, and more spending.

This is about moving away from policies that give short-term sugar hits to consumers and move toward proper long-term investment in businesses that will grow our economy and increase productivity, increase labour demand, employment, and wages.

A similar move has been made by Australia in recent years and provides a credible international model. New Zealand needs to catch up to key competitors to ensure that we are seen as a country of growth for our businesses that innovate and create productivity and employment.

The OECD consistently ranks corporate income taxes among the taxes most harmful to economic growth because they affect investment decisions and capital formation.

It shows that lowering corporate tax rates encourages investment by reducing the cost of capital, and that corporate taxation can have a negative effect on productivity.

New Zealand needs smart long-term thinking to turn our economy around and get our economy growing.

documents/2026-09-26-nzfirst-policy-anno.text:
# NZFirst Policy Announcement: Ending The Waitangi Make-Work Industry

*Saturday, 26 September 2026, 4:33 pm Press Release: New Zealand First Party* — [https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA2609/S00277/nzfirst-policy-announcement-ending-the-waitangi-make-work-industry.htm](https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA2609/S00277/nzfirst-policy-announcement-ending-the-waitangi-make-work-industry.htm)

## Full text

The Treaty of Waitangi Tribunal has become a make-work organisation – now hearing any and all claims that in a former time would’ve been dismissed on application as being inappropriate.

Many claims before the tribunal are directly contesting the right of a mandated parliament to pass laws.

That is a direct semi-judicial threat against the very essence of our democracy. That is why New Zealand First today is announcing its plan to end the Treaty of Waitangi grievance industry and get back to all being equal citizens with equal rights in our country.

New Zealand First will table legislation within the first 100 days after the next election to immediately abolish the Waitangi Tribunal, and replace it with the Treaty of Waitangi Completion Commission.

The new Commission will have the purpose of finalising all claims prior to 2008, after which time its work will be finished.

The Treaty of Waitangi industry jobs will be replaced by real work. The days of the Waitangi Tribunal acting as an authority of parliament will be over.

We will put an end to activists using the Tribunal and taxpayers money as a platform to interfere with the direction and legislation of parliament.

Maori land reform and administrative improvements in the Maori Land Court will be a major priority for New Zealand First.

Under New Zealand First, the Ministry of Maori Development will be directed to drive practical outcomes that accelerate development. The Ministry will ensure that Maori owned land, marine farming, forestry and other resources continue to enhance regional productivity, employment and community resilience.

We will also ensure that all relevant policy issues pertaining to the implementation of existing Treaty of Waitangi settlements are addressed by a strengthened Ministry of Maori Development.

Contemporary claims, modern policy differences, and post-settlement leadership will be the responsibility of the Ministry of Maori Development.

Crown Maori relations work will return to being the responsibility of the Ministry of Maori Development - as was written into the law in 1991 when that department was established.
